prompt: Why does a crystalline solid melt at a sharp temperature, while an amorphous solid such as candle wax softens over a range?

choices.text: In a crystal every unit is held by the same forces, so all attractions break at once; in an amorphous solid the attractions vary, and the weakest break first
Amorphous solids contain no attractive forces between their particles
choices.why: Amorphous solids do have attractions; they are simply unequal, so they break over a range of temperatures.

choices.text: Crystals are always made of ions, while amorphous solids are always made of molecules
choices.why: Crystals can be metallic, covalent network, or molecular too. The key difference is order: identical environments versus a range of environments.

choices.text: Amorphous solids have stronger forces, so they need more heating to melt
choices.why: The issue is not the average strength but the spread. Nonequivalent environments in an amorphous solid give a range of attraction strengths.

explanation: A crystalline solid has a precise melting temperature because each atom or molecule of the same type is held in place by the same forces, so all the attractions require the same energy to break. In an amorphous solid the particles are structurally nonequivalent: some forces are weaker than others, the weakest break first on heating, and the material softens over a range of temperatures.

prompt: Under what conditions does an ionic solid such as NaCl conduct electricity?

choices.text: When molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move
As a solid, because it contains charged ions
choices.why: In the solid, the ions are locked in the lattice and can't move, so solid ionic compounds don't conduct.

choices.text: Never, because ionic compounds contain no free electrons
choices.why: Ions themselves can carry current once they are mobile, in a melt or a solution.

choices.text: Only when cooled to very low temperature
choices.why: Cooling won't free the ions. Melting or dissolving the solid lets the ions move and carry current.

explanation: Ionic solids are composed of positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic attractions. They are hard and brittle with high melting points, and they do not conduct electricity as solids. They do conduct when molten or dissolved, because their ions are free to move.

prompt: A solid is very hard, does not conduct electricity, and has a very high melting point. It is made of atoms of electronegative elements joined to each other throughout the crystal. What type of solid is it?

choices.text: A covalent network solid, like diamond, SiO2, or SiC
An ionic solid
choices.why: Ionic solids are made of ions, not atoms of electronegative elements bonded to each other, and they conduct when molten.

choices.text: A metallic solid
choices.why: Metallic solids are made of electropositive atoms and conduct heat and electricity well.

choices.text: A molecular solid
choices.why: Molecular solids are held by intermolecular forces and have low melting points.

explanation: In covalent network solids the atoms are held together by a network of covalent bonds, so melting requires breaking covalent bonds. They are very hard, not conductive, and have very high melting points; examples are diamond (which melts above 3500 °C), SiO2, and SiC.

prompt: Why do molecular solids made of H2, N2, O2, or F2 melt below −200 °C?

choices.text: These are small nonpolar molecules, so the attractive forces between them are very weak
The covalent bonds within these molecules are very weak
choices.why: Melting a molecular solid doesn't break the bonds inside the molecules. It only overcomes the weak attractions between them.

choices.text: They are ionic solids with small charges
choices.why: These are molecular solids of neutral molecules, not ionic solids.

choices.text: They are amorphous, so they have no definite melting point
choices.why: They are crystalline molecular solids; their low melting points reflect weak intermolecular attractions.

explanation: Molecular solids are composed of neutral molecules held by intermolecular forces. Small symmetrical nonpolar molecules such as H2, N2, O2, and F2 have weak attractive forces and form molecular solids with very low melting points (below −200 °C). Larger nonpolar molecules attract each other more strongly and melt at higher temperatures.

prompt: Graphite is a covalent solid, yet unlike diamond it is soft and electrically conductive. Why?

choices.text: It consists of planar covalent sheets held together in layers by noncovalent forces
Its carbon atoms are held together only by intermolecular forces
choices.why: Within each sheet the carbon atoms are covalently bonded. Only the forces between the layers are noncovalent.

choices.text: It is an ionic solid of C^4+ and C^4− ions
choices.why: Graphite is not ionic. Its softness comes from weak forces between covalent layers.

choices.text: It is an amorphous form of carbon with no regular structure
choices.why: Graphite is crystalline, made of ordered planar sheets of hexagonally bonded carbon.

explanation: Graphite is an exceptional covalent solid, composed of planar sheets of covalently bonded carbon held together in layers by noncovalent forces. The weak attraction between layers lets graphite rub off onto paper, and unlike typical covalent solids it is very soft and electrically conductive. Graphene is a single, one-atom-thick sheet of graphite.

prompt: In a crystal, what is an interstitial defect?

choices.text: An atom or ion sitting in a position between the regular lattice positions
A lattice position that should contain an atom or ion but is empty
choices.why: That is a vacancy.

choices.text: An impurity atom that replaces a regular atom on its lattice site
choices.why: That is a substitutional impurity, as when silicon is doped with other elements.

choices.text: A region of the crystal that has melted
choices.why: Defects are local irregularities in the repeating pattern, not melted regions.

explanation: Vacancies occur when positions that should contain atoms or ions are empty. Less commonly, some atoms or ions occupy interstitial sites, located between the regular positions. Impurities can also distort the structure, and trace impurities are sometimes deliberately added (doping) to produce useful properties, as in silicon for computer chips.

prompt: Which statement about the simple cubic structure is correct?

choices.text: Each atom has a coordination number of 6, the spheres fill about 52% of the space, and polonium is the only metal with this structure
Each atom has a coordination number of 8, and most metals adopt this structure
choices.why: A coordination number of 8 belongs to body-centered cubic. Simple cubic packing is inefficient, and only Po adopts it.

choices.text: Each atom has a coordination number of 12, and the spheres fill 74% of the space
choices.why: Those values describe the closest-packed structures (CCP/FCC and HCP).

choices.text: The unit cell contains two atoms, and the spheres fill 68% of the space
choices.why: Two atoms per cell and 68% filling describe body-centered cubic.

explanation: In a simple cubic structure each atom touches four neighbors in its layer, one above, and one below, for a coordination number of six. The spheres fill only about 52% of the volume, an inefficient arrangement, and only one metal, polonium, crystallizes this way. The unit cell contains 8 × 1/8 = 1 atom.

prompt: How many atoms does a body-centered cubic (BCC) unit cell contain, and what is the coordination number of each atom?

choices.text: Two atoms per cell; coordination number 8
One atom per cell; coordination number 6
choices.why: Those describe simple cubic. BCC adds an atom at the center of the cube.

choices.text: Four atoms per cell; coordination number 12
choices.why: Those describe face-centered cubic (cubic closest packing).

choices.text: Nine atoms per cell; coordination number 8
choices.why: The coordination number is right, but the eight corner atoms are each shared among eight cells, contributing 1 atom in total, plus 1 in the center.

explanation: A BCC unit cell contains one-eighth of an atom at each of the eight corners (8 × 1/8 = 1) plus one atom in the center, for two atoms. The corner atoms don't touch each other but touch the central atom; each atom touches four atoms in the layer above and four in the layer below, giving a coordination number of eight. BCC fills about 68% of the volume.

prompt: How do cubic closest packing (CCP) and hexagonal closest packing (HCP) differ?

choices.text: HCP stacks close-packed layers ABAB…, with the third layer over the first; CCP stacks them ABCABC…, with the third layer over neither of the first two
HCP has a coordination number of 12 and CCP has a coordination number of 8
choices.why: Both closest-packed structures have a coordination number of 12.

choices.text: CCP fills 74% of space while HCP fills only 52%
choices.why: Both are closest-packed arrangements that fill the same fraction of space; 52% is simple cubic.

choices.text: HCP layers are square arrays, while CCP layers are hexagonal
choices.why: Both consist of hexagonally arranged close-packed layers; they differ only in how the layers stack.

explanation: Both types consist of repeating layers of hexagonally arranged atoms, and in both, each atom in the second layer (B) contacts three atoms in the first (A). In HCP the third layer sits directly above the first, giving ABABAB…. In CCP the third layer (C) is above neither, giving ABCABC…. CCP is the same as face-centered cubic, and both closest-packed types give a coordination number of 12.

prompt: Which of these metals crystallizes in a hexagonal closest-packed (HCP) structure?

choices.text: Mg
Cu
choices.why: Cu crystallizes in a cubic closest-packed (FCC) structure, along with Ag, Al, Ca, Ni, Pb, and Pt.

choices.text: W
choices.why: W is one of the body-centered cubic metals, with K, Ba, Cr, Mo, and Fe.

choices.text: Po
choices.why: Po is the only metal with a simple cubic structure.

explanation: Metals that crystallize in an HCP structure include Cd, Co, Mg, and Zn. Metals with a CCP (FCC) structure include Ag, Al, Ca, Cu, Ni, Pb, and Pt, while K, Ba, Cr, Mo, W, and room-temperature Fe are BCC.

prompt: In a simple cubic unit cell, the atoms touch along the edge (edge length = 2r) and the cell contains one atom. What percentage of the cell's volume is filled by the atom? (Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr^3.)
explanation: Filled fraction = (4/3)πr^3 ÷ (2r)^3 = (4/3)π/8 = π/6 = 0.524, or 52.4%. This matches the statement that simple cubic spheres fill only about 52% of the volume.

prompt: Aluminum crystallizes in a face-centered cubic structure, and its atomic radius is 143 pm. In an FCC cell the atoms touch along the face diagonal, so the face diagonal equals 4r. What is the edge length of the unit cell, in pm?
explanation: The face diagonal is a√2 = 4r, so a = 4r/√2 = 2√2 r = 2√2 × 143 pm = 404 pm (404.5 pm).

prompt: Tungsten has a body-centered cubic structure with an edge length of 316.5 pm. In BCC the corner atoms touch the central atom, so the body diagonal of the cube (a√3) equals 4r. What is the atomic radius of tungsten, in pm?
explanation: The body diagonal a√3 contains one radius from each of two opposite corner atoms plus the diameter of the central atom: a√3 = 4r. So r = √3 × 316.5 pm/4 = 137 pm.

prompt: Iron at room temperature has a body-centered cubic structure with an edge length of 286.6 pm. Its molar mass is 55.845 g/mol. What is the density of iron, in g/cm^3?
Copper has a cubic unit cell with an edge length of 361.5 pm, a density of 8.96 g/cm^3, and a molar mass of 63.55 g/mol. How many atoms are in one unit cell? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
explanation: Mass of one cell = density × volume = 8.96 g/cm^3 × (361.5 × 10^−10 cm)^3 = 4.23 × 10^−22 g. Mass of one atom = 63.55 g/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10^23 mol^−1 = 1.055 × 10^−22 g. Atoms per cell = 4.23 × 10^−22 ÷ 1.055 × 10^−22 = 4.01 ≈ 4, which is what a face-centered cubic cell contains (8 × 1/8 + 6 × 1/2).

prompt: A unit cell has edge lengths a = b ≠ c, and all three angles are 90°. Which lattice system is it?

choices.text: Tetragonal
Cubic
choices.why: A cubic cell has a = b = c, with all angles 90°.

choices.text: Orthorhombic
choices.why: An orthorhombic cell has three unequal edges, a ≠ b ≠ c, with all angles 90°.

choices.text: Hexagonal
choices.why: A hexagonal cell has a = b ≠ c, but with γ = 120°.

explanation: A unit cell is defined by its three axis lengths (a, b, c) and the angles between them (α, β, γ). There are seven lattice systems and 14 unit cells. A tetragonal cell has a = b ≠ c with α = β = γ = 90°; cubic has a = b = c; orthorhombic has a ≠ b ≠ c; hexagonal has a = b ≠ c with γ = 120°.

prompt: In a closest-packed (HCP or CCP) array of anions, how many tetrahedral and octahedral holes are there per anion?

choices.text: Two tetrahedral holes and one octahedral hole per anion
One tetrahedral hole and two octahedral holes per anion
choices.why: This is reversed. There are twice as many (smaller) tetrahedral holes as anions, and one (larger) octahedral hole per anion.

choices.text: One of each per anion
choices.why: There is one octahedral hole per anion, but two tetrahedral holes.

choices.text: Four tetrahedral holes and one octahedral hole per anion
choices.why: There are two tetrahedral holes per anion, which is why filling all of them gives a 2:1 cation:anion ratio, as in Li2O.

explanation: There are two tetrahedral holes for each anion in an HCP or CCP array, so filling all of them gives a maximum cation:anion ratio of 2:1 (Li2O, Na2S). The ratio of octahedral holes to anions is 1:1, so filling all of them gives a 1:1 ratio (NiO, NaCl).

prompt: In a compound, cations M occupy one-quarter of the tetrahedral holes in a closest-packed array of anions X. What is the empirical formula?

choices.text: MX2
MX
choices.why: MX would need one-half of the tetrahedral holes filled (as in ZnS), since there are two tetrahedral holes per anion.

choices.text: M2X
choices.why: M2X results from filling all of the tetrahedral holes, as in Li2O.

choices.text: MX4
choices.why: There are two tetrahedral holes per anion, not one, so one-quarter occupancy gives 2 × 1/4 = 1/2 cation per anion.

explanation: There are two tetrahedral holes per anion. If one-quarter are occupied, there are 2 × 1/4 = 1/2 cations per anion, so the ratio M:X is 1:2 and the formula is MX2.

prompt: In a mixed oxide, A ions occupy one-eighth of the tetrahedral holes and B ions occupy one-half of the octahedral holes in a closest-packed array of oxide ions. What is the formula?

choices.text: AB2O4
ABO3
choices.why: Count per oxide ion: A = 2 × 1/8 = 1/4 and B = 1 × 1/2 = 1/2. Multiplying by 4 gives AB2O4, not ABO3.

choices.text: A2BO4
choices.why: This swaps the A and B counts. There are 1/2 B ions per oxide ion but only 1/4 A ions.

choices.text: AB4O8
choices.why: This counts only one tetrahedral hole per oxide ion (A = 1/8 per O). There are two, so A = 2 × 1/8 = 1/4 per O, and the formula is AB2O4.

explanation: Per oxide ion there are two tetrahedral holes and one octahedral hole. A fills one-eighth of the tetrahedral holes: 2 × 1/8 = 1/4 A per O. B fills one-half of the octahedral holes: 1 × 1/2 = 1/2 B per O. The ratio A:B:O = 1/4 : 1/2 : 1 = 1:2:4, giving AB2O4.

prompt: Cations M occupy one-third of the octahedral holes in a closest-packed array of anions X. What is the empirical formula?

choices.text: MX3
M3X
choices.why: This inverts the ratio. With one octahedral hole per anion, one-third occupancy gives 1/3 cation per anion.

choices.text: M2X3
choices.why: M2X3 comes from filling two-thirds of the octahedral holes, as in Al2O3.

choices.text: MX2
choices.why: MX2 corresponds to half of the octahedral holes filled, as in TiO2.

explanation: The ratio of octahedral holes to anions in a closest-packed array is 1:1. With one-third of them occupied, there is 1/3 M per X, so the formula is MX3. For comparison, two-thirds occupancy gives Al2O3 and one-half gives TiO2.

prompt: A cation is about 22.5–41.4% of the anion radius when it fits a tetrahedral hole, 41.4–73.2% for an octahedral hole, and 73.2–100% for a cubic hole. Na^+ has a radius of 102 pm and Cl^− has a radius of 181 pm. Which hole does Na^+ fit?

choices.text: An octahedral hole, since 102/181 = 0.56
A tetrahedral hole, since Na^+ is smaller than Cl^−
choices.why: Being smaller isn't enough; tetrahedral holes suit ratios of 0.225–0.414. Na^+/Cl^− = 0.56 falls in the octahedral range.

choices.text: A cubic hole, since the ions are similar in size
choices.why: Cubic holes suit ratios above 0.732, like Cs^+/Cl^− (174/181 = 0.96). Na^+/Cl^− is only 0.56.

choices.text: No hole; Na^+ is too large for any hole in a Cl^− array
choices.why: Na^+ is much smaller than Cl^−, with a ratio of 0.56, which fits an octahedral hole.

explanation: Relatively small cations occupy tetrahedral holes, larger ones octahedral holes, and cations too large for octahedral holes go into cubic holes in a simple cubic anion array. Na^+/Cl^− = 102/181 = 0.56, in the octahedral range, consistent with NaCl having Na^+ ions in the octahedral holes of an FCC array of Cl^− ions.

prompt: CsCl has a Cl^− ion at each corner of a cubic cell and a Cs^+ ion at the center. Why isn't it a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure?

choices.text: A Cs^+ ion is not identical to a Cl^− ion, so the cell center is not a lattice point; it is a simple cubic lattice
Because the Cs^+ and Cl^− ions don't touch
choices.why: They do touch, along the body diagonals of the cell. The reason is that the center and corner ions are different.

choices.text: Because CsCl has a 1:2 cation:anion ratio
choices.why: The cell contains one Cs^+ and one Cl^−, giving the 1:1 ratio of the formula.

choices.text: Because Cs^+ is much smaller than Cl^−
choices.why: Cs^+ (174 pm) and Cl^− (181 pm) are similar in size, which is why CsCl adopts this structure.

explanation: In CsCl the Cs^+ and Cl^− ions, of similar size, touch along the body diagonals, and one of each is present per cell. There is no lattice point at the center of the cell, because a cesium ion is not identical to a chloride ion, so CsCl is described as simple cubic, not BCC. The cell can equally be drawn with Cs^+ at the corners and Cl^− at the center.

prompt: In the NaCl unit cell, Cl^− ions form an FCC array. Where are the Na^+ ions, and how many formula units does the cell contain?

choices.text: In the octahedral holes, at the edge centers and the cell center; 4 Na^+ and 4 Cl^−
In the tetrahedral holes; 4 Na^+ and 8 Cl^−
choices.why: Filling all tetrahedral holes describes the fluorite (CaF2) arrangement. Na^+ ions fill the octahedral holes, giving 1:1.

choices.text: At the cell center only; 1 Na^+ and 1 Cl^−
choices.why: One ion at the center of a simple cubic cell describes CsCl. In NaCl, Na^+ is also at the 12 edge centers.

choices.text: In half of the tetrahedral holes; 4 Na^+ and 4 Cl^−
choices.why: Half of the tetrahedral holes filled describes zinc blende, ZnS.

explanation: In NaCl, the chloride ions form an FCC cell, with sodium ions in the octahedral holes in the middle of the cell edges and in the center of the cell. The ions touch along the cell edges. The cell contains 12 × 1/4 + 1 = 4 Na^+ and 8 × 1/8 + 6 × 1/2 = 4 Cl^−, matching the 1:1 formula.

prompt: In the CaF2 (fluorite) unit cell, Ca^2+ ions sit on an FCC lattice. Where are the F^− ions?

choices.text: In all of the tetrahedral holes, giving 4 Ca^2+ and 8 F^− per cell
In all of the octahedral holes, giving 4 Ca^2+ and 4 F^−
choices.why: That would give a 1:1 ratio, as in NaCl. CaF2 needs two F^− per Ca^2+, which matches the two tetrahedral holes per lattice ion.

choices.text: In half of the tetrahedral holes, giving 4 Ca^2+ and 4 F^−
choices.why: Half the tetrahedral holes filled is the zinc blende arrangement, which gives 1:1.

choices.text: On the FCC lattice points, with Ca^2+ in the holes
choices.why: In fluorite the cations are on the lattice points. The F^− ions cannot form the lattice because they don't all have identical environments.

explanation: In CaF2 the calcium ions sit on the lattice points of an FCC lattice, and all of the tetrahedral sites are occupied by fluoride ions. The cell contains four Ca^2+ and eight F^−, the 1:2 ratio of the formula. The same structure can be seen as a simple cubic array of F^− ions with Ca^2+ in half of the cubic holes.

prompt: In CsCl, the Cs^+ and Cl^− ions touch along the body diagonal of the cubic unit cell, so the body diagonal (a√3) equals 2(r_Cs + r_Cl). Using r(Cs^+) = 174 pm and r(Cl^−) = 181 pm, what edge length, in pm, does this predict?
explanation: The body diagonal holds one Cs^+ diameter and two Cl^− radii (one from each of two opposite corners), so a√3 = 2(174 + 181) pm = 710 pm. Then a = 710 pm/√3 = 410 pm.

prompt: NaCl has an FCC unit cell containing four NaCl formula units, with an edge length of 564 pm. The molar mass of NaCl is 58.44 g/mol. What is the density of NaCl, in g/cm^3?
Why are X-rays, rather than visible light, used to determine crystal structures by diffraction?

choices.text: Their wavelengths, a few Å, are comparable to the distances between atoms in crystals
They are absorbed completely by crystals, so they can be measured
choices.why: Diffraction requires the waves to be scattered, not absorbed. It happens when the wavelength is comparable to the spacing of the scatterers.

choices.text: Their wavelengths are much longer than the spacing between atoms
choices.why: Visible light has wavelengths far longer than interatomic spacings. X-ray wavelengths are about the same as those spacings.

choices.text: X-rays break the bonds and release the atoms for counting
choices.why: X-ray crystallography measures the angles of diffracted beams; it doesn't count released atoms.

explanation: Diffraction is the change in direction of an electromagnetic wave when it encounters a barrier with dimensions comparable to its wavelength. X-rays have wavelengths about as long as the distance between neighboring atoms in crystals (a few Å), so waves scattered by the atoms interfere constructively or destructively depending on the angle.

prompt: X-rays are diffracted by crystal planes spaced 0.250 nm apart, and the second-order (n = 2) diffraction is observed at θ = 35.0°. Using the Bragg equation, nλ = 2d sinθ, what is the X-ray wavelength, in nm?
A crystal gives a first-order (n = 1) X-ray diffraction peak at θ = 15.0° from a set of planes. At what angle θ, in degrees, will the second-order (n = 2) peak from the same planes appear?
explanation: From nλ = 2d sinθ with λ and d fixed, sinθ is proportional to n: sinθ2 = 2 sinθ1 = 2 × sin(15.0°) = 2 × 0.2588 = 0.5176. So θ2 = arcsin(0.5176) = 31.2°. Doubling n roughly, but not exactly, doubles the angle.
